A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RAD research work. Their text, equations, tables, and figures support comparison. v1 ends with references and has no appendices; v2's Appendices A-F were included in the assessment.

before.justification: v1 reports original RAD results on nine locomotion datasets, component ablations, training curves, and retrieval-parameter experiments.

after.justification: v2 reports original D-RAD and DL-RAD benchmark results, distribution-shift experiments, ablations, runtime measurements, and additional appendix evaluations.

M1.justification: v1 uses scalar step estimation trained with MSE and a state-action diffusion planner. v2 replaces step regression with classification and cross-entropy, adds the DiffuserLite-based DL-RAD variant with state-only generation and inverse dynamics, and describes an expert-filtered retrieval database instead of all dataset states (Sections 4.1-4.4). These change substantive components and procedures.

E1.justification: v2 retains the nine locomotion datasets and adds AntMaze navigation, Maze2D navigation, FrankaKitchen manipulation, and OGBench stitching/explore evaluations. It also evaluates distinct deployment scenarios involving shifted initial states and previously unseen maze regions (Section 5.2; Appendices D.5 and D.10).

E2.justification: In the shared locomotion comparison, v2 adds CQL, IQL, MOPO, MOReL, SER, DiffStitch, and DiffuserLite, while removing CEIL, ReDiffuser, and TT. Additional comparisons introduce direct retrieval combination (DRC) and the OGBench comparators GCBC, GCIVL, GCIQL, QRL, CRL, and HIQL (Tables 8 and 17).

E3.justification: v2 introduces controlled evaluation protocols using Random-dataset initializations, 0%/20% regional training coverage, and baselines trained on the same expert subset. New DL-RAD experiments use distinct planning horizons, while runtime studies compare per-step, full-rollout, and fixed-step costs and 1-step versus 10-step replanning. These are added experimental settings, not evidence that v1's experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The original component-ablation ideas remain under renamed labels, and the similarity-threshold sweep moves to Appendix D.4. v2 adds backbone and naive-retrieval controls, expert-subset controls, OOD stress tests, ranking and similarity-metric sensitivity, periodic replanning, and trajectory visualizations. v1's training-curve comparison and k=6/30/60/120 candidate-count sweep are removed.

E5.justification: Table 1 changes uncertainty reporting from standard deviations in v1 to standard errors in v2, while both specify three random seeds. The retained similarity-threshold results lose their uncertainty estimates (v1 Table 2 versus v2 Table 9). An increase in run count is not documented.

E6.justification: The nine original RAD task means are retained as D-RAD, but v2 adds extensive DL-RAD, navigation, manipulation, OGBench, OOD, ablation, and timing results. For example, DL-RAD has a newly reported locomotion average of 87.5. The DS locomotion average changes from 77.0 to 81.1 despite unchanged task scores, correcting the aggregate. New variants and settings do not establish a same-setting improvement of the original RAD.

T1.justification: v2 adds Appendix E's chain-rule derivation that target conditioning cannot increase conditional trajectory entropy. It also corrects the return-to-go discount exponent from i to i-t in the problem definition. These provide a limited theoretical addition and correction; the entropy argument does not establish a policy-performance guarantee.

C1.justification: The central claims remain that retrieving high-return targets guides generative planning out of OOD or low-return regions without static augmentation, yielding competitive or superior offline-RL performance. The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain this contribution; the expanded experiments primarily provide additional support.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands interpretations concerning heterogeneous data quality, limited gains on expert data, target reachability, robustness to imperfect retrieval, and why long remaining trajectories provide useful planning anchors. It adds runtime tradeoffs and qualifications about experimental scope. Dependence on available high-return states remains, while v1's discussion of stochastic retrieval failures and global-planning extensions is dropped.

D1.justification: Beyond v1's brief implementation settings, v2 supplies training/inference pseudocode, U-Net and DiT specifications, expert-subset selection rules, domain-specific horizons, retrieval counts, runtime/memory measurements, and a code-access link (Appendices B-D). However, v1's explicit 20 denoising steps and four-layer step-network specification are not retained.

R1.justification: v2 substantially revises positioning around conservative offline RL, generative planning, and augmentation, adding discussion of DiffStitch and DiffuserLite while dropping treatments of works such as AWAC, BAIL, CRR, and COMBO. Appendix F explicitly distinguishes RAD's decision-time planning from DiffStitch's offline augmentation and explains their potential compatibility.

P1.justification: The related work, preliminaries, method, and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten and reorganized. Diffusion background precedes the problem definition; the method is organized around TS, SE, and PL; experiments follow explicit research questions; and retained parameter analysis moves into new appendices. Terminology and contribution presentation also change throughout.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column main-text layout, redraws Figures 1-2, and restructures Figure 3 with separate task panels, revised axes, and an added control. The training-curve figure is replaced by navigation rollouts, return-distribution plots are added, and Table 1 becomes a multidomain comparison. Numerous new tables and algorithm displays substantially alter presentation.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses v1's central evidential gap: OOD-generalization claims previously rested on ordinary locomotion evaluations. Direct distribution-shift tests, naive-retrieval and expert-subset controls, broader tasks, computational-cost measurements, and fuller implementation details substantially strengthen empirical support and reproducibility. Some original analyses and uncertainty estimates disappear, and Appendix E's entropy inequality alone does not justify improved prediction accuracy. These limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains.
